scenes.title: Discover events with a schema registry
scenes.narration: This slide starts with a problem developers often face: an application publishes events, but how do consumers know their structure? Look at the example event in the middle. It includes job ID, status and model ID for a model job. EventBridge Schema Registry can discover a schema from events, and the version-one panel shows these fields with their types. Now follow the next version. The event evolves and adds token count, a numeric field. Rather than changing the old schema without a trace, we can register a new schema version that includes the additional field. The right side shows generated code bindings for languages such as Python, Java or TypeScript. A consumer can then access event properties through typed classes instead of manually guessing JSON field names. This is especially useful when multiple teams share event contracts. There is a practical detail worth adding: generated bindings do not automatically make every producer compatible with every consumer. Treat required fields, optional fields and version compatibility as design decisions. The message to remember is that schema discovery documents what events contain, while schema versioning and code generation make changes easier for consumers to understand.

scenes.title: SNS topic and subscriptions
scenes.narration: Here the key idea is fan-out: one published alert can reach several independent subscribers. Start on the left. A model-evaluation service detects that quality has fallen below a threshold and publishes a message to the SNS topic called model-eval-alerts. The topic then sends separate copies to three subscriptions: an email address, an SQS queue and a Lambda function. Follow each branch. Email informs a person, the queue holds a copy for asynchronous processing, and Lambda can take an automated action. All three receive the same published event through their own delivery paths. Now compare the two panels below the architecture. SNS fan-out is not the same as several consumers polling one SQS queue. With SNS, each matching subscription receives its own copy. With competing SQS consumers, one message is normally processed by just one of those workers. For a GenAI system, SNS can notify the operations team and separately trigger remediation whenever model evaluation fails. Subscription filters can narrow which messages a subscriber receives, but a topic itself is not a durable work queue. Use SNS for independent notification paths; use SQS for buffered worker processing.

scenes.title: SNS fan-out and delivery path
scenes.narration: This slide takes the fan-out idea one step further and shows why separating delivery paths improves reliability. At the top, the producer publishes one alert to an SNS topic. Three arrows leave the topic: one goes to an audit SQS queue, another to a remediation SQS queue, and the third to an email subscription. Each branch has its own downstream job. Audit workers can log, store or analyse alerts; remediation workers can execute a playbook; and the operations team receives an email for awareness. Look at the boxes beneath the two queues. Worker groups can scale according to their own queue depth, process messages independently, and use retries or dead-letter queues when a message repeatedly fails. The email branch has its own delivery retries and may fail without stopping the SQS consumers. That's the key reliability point: the same alert fans out, but one slow subscriber should not force all other consumers to stop. An SNS subscription can fail to deliver even if publishing succeeded, so monitor delivery outcomes and configure retry or dead-letter behavior appropriate to each endpoint type. The result shown at the bottom is three independent outcomes from one source alert.

scenes.title: Protect SNS notifications
scenes.narration: This diagram is about securing both sides of SNS delivery. The first panel shows publisher permission. An SNS topic resource policy defines which trusted roles or AWS services may call Publish, and can restrict callers with conditions such as the expected account or source. Follow the example in the middle: an unauthorised publisher is denied, while an authorised service can submit an alert to the topic. Next look at subscriber endpoint permission. Delivering a message to SQS or Lambda may require a resource-based policy on that destination that explicitly allows the SNS topic. Giving someone permission to publish does not automatically grant SNS permission to invoke every subscriber. The right side adds transport and storage protection. HTTPS protects deliveries to HTTPS endpoints in transit; when configured, KMS encryption helps protect topic data at rest. For a customer-managed key, compatible key policies are required for the principals and services involved. This layered model matters when alerts contain operational or AI-related metadata. Keep sensitive details to the minimum necessary, and secure the topic and destination independently. Remember three distinct checks: who can publish, where SNS may deliver, and how the information is protected.

scenes.title: Move SaaS data with Amazon AppFlow
scenes.narration: Our final slide in this video shows how external business data reaches an AWS analytics or GenAI workflow. Follow the pipeline from left to right. Customer information or knowledge records begin in a SaaS CRM application. Amazon AppFlow connects to that source using supported connector credentials, selects records and maps fields into a usable format. Next, choose when the flow runs: perhaps on a schedule, or based on a supported source event when the connector allows that mode. AppFlow then exports the selected records to an S3 destination. The right-hand stage represents downstream preparation and knowledge-base ingestion, where the exported data might be cleaned, chunked and indexed for retrieval. The example output refers to customer FAQ records stored as CSV or JSON. Look at the connector examples below, such as Salesforce, HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Shopify and Zendesk. The exact triggers and objects supported vary by connector, so this is not a promise that every source works in every mode. AppFlow moves and transforms supported SaaS data; it doesn't automatically create a high-quality knowledge base. Later processing must still handle permissions, sensitive records, freshness and indexing.
